result: The authors developed and applied a nanoPOTS-based single-cell proteomics method to analyze E15 chicken utricle hair cells and supporting cells. FM1-43 labeling distinguished hair cells (FM1-43high, ~1 picoliter volume) from supporting cells (FM1-43low, ~0.67 picoliter volume). Single FM1-43high cells yielded ~200 unique peptides and ~60 proteins, while pools of 20 cells yielded ~2500 peptides and ~600 proteins. The method showed low keratin contamination (~0.1% of total iBAQ) and nonlinear scaling of total iBAQ with cell number, suggesting protein loss to surface adsorption.
evaluation: Claims C2-C57 collectively describe the technical implementation and performance characteristics of the nanoPOTS single-cell proteomics method. The data show consistent measurements of cell volumes, peptide/protein identifications scaling with cell number, and quality control metrics (keratin contamination, noise discrimination). The nonlinear iBAQ scaling (C47-C48) is appropriately interpreted as protein loss, supported by the large nanowell-to-cell volume ratio (C49). Sample sizes are reported (N=5-10 for volume measurements, N=4-5 for proteomics replicates).

result: Proteomics analysis of pooled cells (20 cells) revealed differential protein expression between hair cells and supporting cells. Hair-cell markers (OCM, CALB2, MYO6) were significantly enriched in FM1-43high cells, while supporting cell markers (TMSB4X, STMN2, SH3BGRL, MARCKS) were enriched in FM1-43low cells. Quantitative analysis showed ACTG1 (total actin) at riBAQ 0.043±0.001 in hair cells vs 0.060±0.005 in supporting cells (p=0.05), while TMSB4X was 0.006±0.002 in hair cells vs 0.056±0.012 in supporting cells (p<0.001, 10-fold difference). The 1:1 stoichiometry of TMSB4X:actin binding suggests sufficient TMSB4X to sequester most actin monomers in supporting cells.
evaluation: Claims C58-C71 present quantitative proteomics data with appropriate statistical analysis (mixed-effects model accounting for intra-sample correlations, Table 1). The key finding that TMSB4X concentration differs significantly from actin in hair cells (p=0.001) but not in supporting cells (p=0.660) is statistically robust. The inference about TMSB4X sequestering actin (C71) is reasonable given the known 1:1 stoichiometry (C70, cited) and the quantitative measurements, though it assumes no other high-abundance actin-binding proteins are present.

result: Quantitative analysis estimated that E15 hair cells contain ~72±8 stereocilia per cell (N=26) and ~15,000,000 total actin molecules, yielding ~200,000 actin molecules per stereocilium. This is fewer than the 400,000 molecules per E20 stereocilium reported previously, consistent with the relative immaturity of E15 cells.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 present calculations based on direct measurements (stereocilia counts, C72) and proteomics quantitation (total actin, C73). The per-stereocilium calculation (C74) assumes nearly all actin is in stereocilia, which is supported by cited literature (Tilney and Tilney, 1988). The comparison to E20 cells (C75) provides developmental context. The calculations are straightforward and the assumptions are explicitly stated and referenced.

result: Single-cell proteomics data (75 proteins detected in ≥5 cells, 62% non-detects, 83% log-normal distributed) were analyzed using CellTrails trajectory analysis. Cells segregated by FM1-43 uptake in lower-dimensional space, with some misclassifications attributed to FM1-43 not being a perfect proxy for maturity. A developmental trajectory was established despite sampling primarily from trajectory endpoints (gap at midpoint pseudotime). Supporting cell markers (AGR3, TMSB4X) decreased along pseudotime while hair cell markers (OCM, CALB2, MYO6, CKB, GAPDH) increased.
evaluation: Claims C77-C95 describe the first application of trajectory analysis to single-cell proteomics data. The data characteristics (C78-C79) are appropriate for the analysis methods used. The CellTrails method was previously validated for transcriptomics (C80, cited). The observation that some cells misclassify (C82-C83) is appropriately interpreted as either technical issues or transitional states (C84-C86), with supporting citations. The limitation of sampling primarily trajectory endpoints (C91-C92) is acknowledged, yet sufficient cells were sampled to establish a trajectory (C93). The systematic changes in protein expression (C94-C95) validate the trajectory.

result: Single-cell RNA-seq of 384 E15 utricle cells using 186 assay genes (182 from prior study plus TMSB4X, AGR3, GPX2, AK1) revealed nine cellular subgroups. After removing stromal cells (S8-S9, identified by lack of TECTA and high TMSB4X), 254 cells mapped to a bifurcating trajectory with one supporting cell branch (TECTA+, OTOA+) and two hair cell branches downstream of ATOH1 peak. The lower-right branch (TrS, striolar) was enriched for LOXHD1, ATP2B2, TMC2, TNNC2, MYO3A, OCM and populated by lateral cells. The upper-right branch split into TrES (extrastriolar, SYN3+, SKOR2+, CALB2+, TMC1+) and TrES* (ATP2B2 enriched, SKOR2 reduced), replicating previous RT-qPCR results.
evaluation: Claims C96-C110 describe comprehensive scRNA-seq analysis with appropriate sample size (384 cells) and validated methodology (Smart-seq protocol, CellTrails analysis). The trajectory reconstruction uses a defined gene set (C97, Table 3) that includes both previously validated genes and newly identified candidates from proteomics. Cell type assignments are based on multiple marker genes with consistent expression patterns (C104-C108). The spatial validation using lateral vs medial origin (C109) provides orthogonal confirmation of cell type assignments. The conclusion that this replicates prior RT-qPCR work (C110) is supported by consistent identification of the same cell types and trajectories.

result: scRNA-seq confirmed that TMSB4X and AGR3 are specific to progenitor cells while GSTO1, GPX2, CRABP1, and AK1 are specific to hair cells. GPX2 and AK1 concentrated in striolar hair cells, while CRABP1 enriched in extrastriolar cells (particularly TrES*). GSTO1 showed similar expression in both hair cell types. Database analysis (gEAR) indicated Gpx2 and Ak1 are enriched in mouse utricle hair cells, while Gsto1 is higher in non-hair cells.
evaluation: Claims C111-C118 validate proteomics findings using orthogonal scRNA-seq data. The cell-type specificity assignments (C111-C112) are consistent between methods. The spatial/subtype enrichment patterns (C113-C115) provide additional resolution beyond the proteomics. The hypothesis connecting high CRABP1 cells to TrES* (C116) is appropriately presented as speculation. The mouse database comparison (C117-C118) shows partial conservation (Gpx2, Ak1) but also species differences (Gsto1), which is reasonable given chicken vs mouse comparison.

result: TMSB4X protein was abundant in supporting cells but not hair cells, with expression decreasing during hair cell differentiation as revealed by proteomics trajectory analysis. scRNA-seq confirmed that TMSB4X transcripts are downregulated when ATOH1 transcription is activated, with substantial decrease during differentiation and near-undetectable levels in striolar hair cells. TMSB4X remained detectable at low levels in TrES cells compared to TrES*.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 and C119-C121 present convergent evidence from proteomics and transcriptomics for TMSB4X downregulation during hair cell differentiation. The proteomics trajectory analysis (C28-C29) is validated by scRNA-seq showing coordinated downregulation with ATOH1 activation (C30), a known master regulator of hair cell differentiation (C31). The observation of differential TMSB4X levels between hair cell subtypes (C121) adds biological nuance. The multi-modal evidence (protein, mRNA, trajectory analysis, immunocytochemistry in C202-C203) provides strong support.

result: Immunocytochemistry validated proteomics findings: AGR3 labeled supporting cells (elongated morphology, no OTOF overlap), CRABP1 was specific for hair cells (OTOF overlap), and TMSB4X was strong in supporting cells but substantially reduced in hair cells. The TMSB4X antibody was validated against mouse TMSB4X, and chicken TMSB4X differs by only two amino acid substitutions. JLA20 (G-actin probe) showed comparable labeling in most cells with increased signal at hair cell bases.
evaluation: Claims C198-C205 provide orthogonal validation of proteomics findings using immunocytochemistry. The AGR3 and CRABP1 localizations (C198-C200) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 3A-F with appropriate positive (OTOF) and negative controls. The TMSB4X antibody validation is appropriate (C201, prior knockdown validation cited), and the protein sequence similarity justifies cross-species use. The TMSB4X localization (C202) matches proteomics data (C203). The JLA20 results (C204-C205) provide additional context about G-actin distribution, though the interpretation is more complex than TMSB4X.

result: scRNA-seq revealed striking ACTB downregulation during hair cell differentiation (>10-fold higher in progenitors than hair cells), with largest decrease in extrastriolar cells. This was partially compensated by modest ACTG1 increase, especially in TrES cells, though ACTG1 remained lower than ACTB overall. The sum of ACTB and ACTG1 transcripts in E15 hair cells was one-quarter that in supporting cells, yet total actin protein levels were similar between cell types, suggesting reduced actin synthesis during differentiation. The two actin isoforms could not be distinguished by mass spectrometry due to detection of only one distinguishing peptide.
evaluation: Claims C122-C129 and C186-C190 describe actin isoform dynamics with appropriate caveats. The scRNA-seq data (C122-C126) show clear trends replicated in prior data (C126, cited). The technical limitation of mass spectrometry (C127-C129) is honestly reported—only one distinguishing peptide detected, preventing isoform-specific quantitation. The calculation that total actin transcripts decrease 4-fold (C188) while protein levels remain similar (C189) is internally consistent and leads to a reasonable inference about reduced synthesis (C190), though this is appropriately presented as speculation. The discrepancy between transcript and protein could also reflect differences in protein stability or other post-transcriptional regulation.

result: GAPDH protein increased during hair cell maturation (proteomics trajectory analysis) while its mRNA remained constant (prior reports), suggesting post-transcriptional regulation. Given that GAPDH concentrates in stereocilia, protein stabilization there is the most likely explanation. This observation highlights the power of protein-based trajectory analysis, as poor correlation between transcript and protein levels means understanding developmental protein changes requires direct measurement rather than inference from RNA-seq.
evaluation: Claims C178-C185 present a clear example of protein-mRNA discordance revealed by single-cell proteomics. The GAPDH protein increase (C178, Figure 4E-F) contrasts with constant mRNA (C179, cited). The inference of post-transcriptional regulation (C180) is reasonable, and the proposed mechanism of protein stabilization in stereocilia (C181-C182) is logical given GAPDH's known localization (cited). The broader conclusion about the value of proteomics (C183-C185) is well-supported by this example and the general principle of poor transcript-protein correlation (C184, cited). This represents a clear advantage of the proteomics approach.

result: The data are consistent with a model that ACTB is sequestered with TMSB4X in supporting cells, and upon differentiation to hair cells, ACTB is made immediately available for stereocilia elongation by degradation of TMSB4X, while ACTG1 expression increases to provide actin for other assemblies (cuticular plate, circumferential belt).
evaluation: Claims C32, C135, and C197 present a mechanistic model integrating multiple observations: TMSB4X abundance in supporting cells (C28, C65-C66), TMSB4X:actin stoichiometry (C70-C71), TMSB4X downregulation during differentiation (C29, C119), ACTB localization to stereocilia (C191, cited), and ACTG1 distribution to all F-actin assemblies (C192, cited). While the model is plausible and consistent with the data, it remains speculative. Key missing evidence includes: (1) direct demonstration of TMSB4X degradation (only decreased expression is shown), (2) causal relationship between TMSB4X loss and actin availability, (3) direct measurement of actin monomer pools, and (4) functional validation through perturbation experiments. The model is appropriately presented as a hypothesis ('consistent with,' 'plausible hypothesis') rather than a proven mechanism.

result: Single-cell proteomics identified unique protein constellations distinguishing hair cells from progenitor cells and enabled de novo reconstruction of a developmental trajectory. Proteins greatly increasing during differentiation included OCM, CRABP1, GPX2, AK1, and GSTO1, while TMSB4X and AGR3 decreased. Several proteins not previously highlighted as cell-type specific were identified.
evaluation: Claims C4-C7 and C133-C134 summarize the major findings. The identification of unique protein constellations (C4) is demonstrated by volcano plot analysis (Figure 2B) and heat maps (Figure 2A). The trajectory reconstruction (C5) is shown in Figure 4 with systematic changes in protein expression (C94-C95). The specific proteins increasing (C6, OCM, CRABP1, GPX2, AK1, GSTO1) and decreasing (C7, TMSB4X, AGR3) are validated by both proteomics and scRNA-seq. The novelty claim (C133-C134) is supported—while some proteins were known (OCM, CALB2, MYO6 for hair cells), others (CRABP1, GSTO1, GPX2, AK1, AGR3, TMSB4X) represent new cell-type markers.

result: Complementary single-cell transcriptome profiling showed corresponding mRNA changes during hair cell maturation. Single-cell proteomics can reveal features of cellular development that may be missed with transcriptomics, particularly proteins that change in expression level without alterations in transcript levels.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C176 articulate the complementary value of proteomics and transcriptomics. The scRNA-seq validation (C8) is demonstrated for multiple proteins (TMSB4X, AGR3, GSTO1, GPX2, CRABP1, AK1). The key advantage of proteomics (C9, C176) is exemplified by GAPDH (C178-C182), where protein increases while mRNA remains constant. This is a well-supported conclusion given the known poor correlation between transcript and protein levels (C184, cited) and the specific examples provided. The claim is appropriately nuanced—proteomics reveals features that 'may be missed' rather than claiming transcriptomics is inadequate.

result: The nanoPOTS method overcomes previous limitations of single-cell proteomics (protein adsorption, lack of amplification) and permits detection of abundant proteins from very small cells (<1 picoliter). However, fewer proteins were detected from single hair cells (~60) than from larger HeLa cells (~700), which is expected given the 5-fold volume difference. The detected proteins represent a small fraction of the total proteome (~3000 proteins in bulk utricle samples, ~13,643 genes expressed by scRNA-seq), limited by the dynamic range of mass spectrometers. Significant protein loss to nanowell surfaces was observed (nonlinear iBAQ scaling), indicating that improved protein recovery is critical for increasing proteome coverage.
evaluation: Claims C130-C149 provide context and acknowledge limitations. The historical challenges (C130, cited) and nanoPOTS capabilities (C131) are appropriately referenced. The comparison to HeLa cells (C136-C138) is fair given the volume difference (C137, measured). The acknowledgment that detected proteins are a small fraction of the total (C139-C145) is honest and well-supported by comparisons to bulk proteomics and scRNA-seq. The inference of protein loss from nonlinear scaling (C147-C148) is reasonable and leads to appropriate conclusions about needed improvements (C149). These limitations do not invalidate the results but properly contextualize the method's current capabilities.

result: This represents the first use of single-cell protein mass spectrometry data to construct a developmental trajectory. Despite being limited to 30 cells, CellTrails generated a trajectory discriminating distinct expression patterns, with endpoint proteins systematically changing as expected. The small sample size likely precluded detection of branching trajectories (TrS, TrES, TrES*) seen with transcriptomics. CellTrails is suitable for single-cell proteomics trajectory analysis, though the field is in its infancy and improvements in sensitivity and reproducibility will enhance future analyses.
evaluation: Claims C164-C173 assess the trajectory analysis achievement and limitations. The novelty claim (C164) appears valid—no prior examples of protein-based single-cell trajectory analysis are cited. The success with limited data (C165, 30 cells) demonstrates feasibility, with appropriate validation (C166-C167). The failure to detect branching (C168) is honestly reported with reasonable explanation (C169, small sample size). The conclusion that CellTrails is suitable (C171) is supported by the successful trajectory reconstruction, though the caveat about the field's infancy (C170) and need for improvements (C172-C173) appropriately tempers enthusiasm. The assessment is balanced and realistic.

result: Potential improvements to the method include fabricating smaller nanowells (though FACS delivery would be challenging), coating surfaces with antifouling materials, or using TMT multiplex labeling with carrier cells. The TMT-nanoPOTS combination significantly increases proteome coverage and throughput. However, mass spectrometry throughput remains a bottleneck, and scRNA-seq will likely continue to offer higher throughput and depth. Future single-cell proteomics may enable analysis of post-translational modifications like phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C150-C154 and C173-C177 discuss future directions with appropriate citations. The technical suggestions (C150-C152) are reasonable, with honest assessment of challenges (C151). The TMT approach (C153-C154) is supported by citations showing its effectiveness. The acknowledgment that scRNA-seq will remain superior for throughput (C175) is realistic. The speculation about future PTM analysis (C177) is appropriately presented as a possibility rather than a promise. These forward-looking statements are grounded in current technical realities and cited literature.

result: The nanoPOTS method detected much higher levels of small proteins (<20 kD) than previous experiments with the same tissue, attributed to processing without transfer steps that cause small protein loss. OCM (formerly parvalbumin 3) is the most abundant protein in E15 chick hair cells (>10% of total protein molecules on a molar basis). Small proteins are not over-represented; cytoskeletal protein levels are similar to bulk experiments. Membrane proteins are underrepresented (a general limitation of shotgun mass spectrometry), partly due to their generally low expression levels.
evaluation: Claims C155-C163 characterize the proteomics data composition. The improved small protein detection (C155-C156) is a reasonable inference given the lack of transfer steps, supported by citation about small protein loss in other methods (C156). The OCM abundance finding (C157-C158) is a clear quantitative result from the data. The assessment that small proteins are not over-represented (C159) is supported by comparison to bulk data for cytoskeletal proteins (C160, cited). The membrane protein underrepresentation (C161-C163) is honestly acknowledged as a general limitation of the method (C161, cited) with reasonable explanation (C162). These characterizations appropriately contextualize the data.

result: In chicken auditory hair cells, ACTB localizes nearly exclusively to stereocilia F-actin cores while ACTG1 distributes to all F-actin assemblies. In mice, Actb or Actg1 knockout results in normal initial stereocilia development (suggesting interchangeability), but aging phenotypes differ due to the proteins themselves rather than expression dynamics. The reduced actin gene expression is consistent with Tilney's model that each hair cell uses an equivalent-sized actin bolus, though an alternative model suggests the final actin amount depends on crosslinker expression levels.
evaluation: Claims C191-C196 integrate the current findings with prior literature on actin isoforms. The chicken isoform localization (C191-C192) and mouse knockout phenotypes (C193-C194) are appropriately cited. The comparison to Tilney's model (C195) and alternative crosslinker model (C196) provides theoretical context for interpreting the reduced actin expression findings (C186-C190). These claims appropriately synthesize current and prior work without overstating conclusions. The presentation acknowledges multiple possible models rather than claiming definitive support for one.

result: Background and contextual claims about hair cell biology, prior methods, and general principles of proteomics and actin dynamics.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C10-C27, C31, C33-C34, C51, C59-C60, C70, C80, C84-C90, C126-C127, C139-C141, C145, C161, C163, C184, C191-C194, C204, C206-C209) represent established knowledge, cited literature, or general principles that provide context for the study. They are appropriately referenced and do not constitute novel findings. They support the rationale and interpretation of the experimental work but are not primary results of this study.
